Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then

$$\|\tau_h f-f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(h \to 0).$$

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be a function.
The **translate** of $f$ by $h$ is the function $\tau_h f$ defined by

$$ (\tau_h f)(x) := f(x-h)\qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

This fixes the sign convention used throughout the page: translating by $h$
shifts the graph of $f$ in the positive $h$-direction.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For fixed $t$, the integrand in the definition of $q_\epsilon(t)$ is strongly measurable and has integrable norm on the compact support of the kernel, so [F2] defines the Bochner integral. A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Substituting this expression into the right-hand side gives $2\|x\|_H^2-2(x,y)_H=2(x-y,x)_H$ by bilinearity. This is the stated identity.

derivations.claim: If $X=\{0\}$, the right-kernel hypothesis forces $Y=\{0\}$; the only $F\in Y^*$ is zero and $x=0$ is the unique solution. If $Y=\{0\}$ and $X\ne\{0\}$, the inf-sup hypothesis fails for any nonzero $x$, so no such instance satisfies the assumptions. Assume henceforth both spaces are nonzero. For each $x\in X$, the functional $y\mapsto b(x,y)$ is bounded and linear. By [F1], let $Sx\in Y$ be the unique vector satisfying $(Sx,y)_Y=b(x,y)$ for every $y\in Y$. Bilinearity and uniqueness make $S:X\to Y$ linear, and the Riesz norm identity gives $\|Sx\|_Y=\sup_{\|y\|_Y\le1}|b(x,y)|\le C_b\|x\|_X$, where $C_b$ is a continuity bound for $b$.

The inf-sup assumption gives $\|Sx\|_Y\ge\beta\|x\|_X$. Thus $S$ is injective. If $Sx_n\to y$ in $Y$, then $\|x_n-x_m\|_X\le\beta^{-1}\|Sx_n-Sx_m\|_Y$, so completeness of $X$ gives $x_n\to x$ for some $x\in X$. The bound in step 1.1 gives $Sx_n\to Sx$, hence $y=Sx$. Therefore $S(X)$ is closed.

If $y\in S(X)^\perp$, then $(Sx,y)_Y=b(x,y)=0$ for every $x\in X$; the right-kernel hypothesis gives $y=0$. Apply [F2] to the closed subspace $S(X)$. Its orthogonal complement is zero, so $Y=S(X)\oplus\{0\}=S(X)$; therefore $S$ is onto.

For the given $F\in Y^*$, let $g\in Y$ be its Riesz representative, so $F(y)=(y,g)_Y$ and $\|g\|_Y=\|F\|_{Y^*}$. Surjectivity supplies $x\in X$ with $Sx=g$, whence $b(x,y)=(Sx,y)_Y=(g,y)_Y=(y,g)_Y=F(y)$ for all $y$, using symmetry of the real inner product. The lower bound $\beta\|x\|_X\le\|Sx\|_Y=\|F\|_{Y^*}$ proves the estimate and also uniqueness.

Let $V$ and $H$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective,
continuous linear map with dense range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real linear
dual of $V$. Identify $H$ with its Hilbert dual by its inner product and embed
$H$ into $V^*$ by
$$h\longmapsto\bigl(v\longmapsto (h,i v)_H\bigr).$$
The resulting dense continuous embeddings are written
$$V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^*\hookrightarrow V^*$$
and $(V,H,V^*)$ is called an **evolution triple**. The pairing between $V^*$
and $V$ is denoted $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$.

For a Hilbert space $X$, $L^2(0,T;X)$ is the space of equivalence classes of
strongly measurable $X$-valued functions $w$ with
$$\int_0^T\|w(t)\|_X^2\,dt<\infty.$$
Strong measurability means being an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of
measurable simple functions. For $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$,
say that $g$ is the **weak time derivative** of $u$ when
$$\int_0^T (i u(t),i v)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. The derivative is
unique up to equality almost everywhere. The **parabolic energy space** is
$$W(0,T;V):=\{u\in L^2(0,T;V):u'\in L^2(0,T;V^*)\},$$
with norm
$$\|u\|_{W(0,T;V)}:=\bigl(\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2+ \|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$
No endpoint values are part of this definition; they are assigned only after
a continuous $H$ trace representative has been proved. Separability is an
additional hypothesis when it is needed by a later result.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space, let
$q\in L^2(\mathbb R;X)$ be strongly measurable, and let $(\eta_\epsilon)$ be
a nonnegative smooth mollifier family of mass one. Define
$$q_\epsilon(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}\eta_\epsilon(t-s)q(s)\,ds.$$
Then each $q_\epsilon$ is smooth with values in $X$ and
$$\|q_\epsilon-q\|_{L^2(\mathbb R;X)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(\epsilon\downarrow0).$$

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

derivations.claim: Let $g_1,g_2\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$ both satisfy [F1], and put $h=g_1-g_2$. For every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$, $\int\langle h(t),v\rangle\phi(t)\,dt=0$. Therefore every Bochner convolution of the zero extension, $h_\epsilon(t)=\int_0^T h(s)\eta_\epsilon(t-s)\,ds$, vanishes on any compact subinterval whose distance from $\{0,T\}$ exceeds $\epsilon$: its scalar pairing against each $v$ is the zero distribution tested by $s\mapsto\eta_\epsilon(t-s)$. By [F2], $h_\epsilon\to h$ in local $L^2(V^*)$, so $h=0$ almost everywhere.

Regard $u$ as a $V^*$-valued function through the continuous embedding $V\hookrightarrow V^*$ and set $G(t)=\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$. The Bochner integral exists by [F3], and [F5] gives $g\in L^1(0,T;V^*)$. For each fixed $v\in V$, [F4] and scalar integration by parts show that $G$ has weak derivative $g$ in the sense of [F1]. Thus $w:=u-G$ has zero distribution derivative. For any $\psi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$ with integral zero, its primitive is compactly supported in $(0,T)$, hence $\int w(t)\psi(t)\,dt=0$ in $V^*$. Fix $\eta\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$ with integral one and put $c=\int w(t)\eta(t)\,dt$. Subtracting $(\int\psi)\eta$ shows $\int(w-c)\psi=0$ for every test $\psi$. The convolutions of $w-c$ are therefore zero on compact subintervals as in step 1.1; [F2] makes them converge to $w-c$ in local $L^2(V^*)$. Hence $w=c$ almost everywhere, and $\widetilde u(t):=c+G(t)$ is a continuous $V^*$ representative of $u$.

Reflect the $V$-valued $L^2$ class evenly to $(-T,2T)$ across $0$ and $T$, and reflect $g$ oddly. The continuous $V^*$ representative from step 2.1 has matching values at each seam. Integration by parts on the three intervals therefore shows that the reflected function has weak $V^*$ derivative equal to the odd reflection of $g$; the endpoint terms cancel, so there are no point masses. Extend both functions by zero beyond $(-T,2T)$. For $0<\epsilon<T/2$, the convolution on the resulting neighborhood of $[0,T]$ does not see the extension jumps at $-T$ or $2T$.

Let $\eta_\epsilon$ be a nonnegative smooth mollifier of mass one, supported in $(-\epsilon,\epsilon)$, and convolve the reflected functions in time. On a neighborhood of $[0,T]$, $u_\epsilon=\eta_\epsilon*u$ is smooth with values in $V$ by [F2]. Testing the reflected weak derivative identity against a fixed $v\in V$ and integrating by parts in the scalar variable gives $\langle u_\epsilon'(t),v\rangle=\int\langle g(s),v\rangle \eta_\epsilon(t-s)\,ds=\langle(\eta_\epsilon*g)(t),v\rangle$. The bounded inclusion $V\to V^*$ commutes with the Bochner integral by [F3], so $u_\epsilon'=\eta_\epsilon*g$ in $V^*$.

Apply the $L^2$ approximation in [F2] to the reflected $V$-valued function and its $V^*$ derivative, then restrict to $(0,T)$. This gives $u_\epsilon\to u$ in $L^2(V)$ and $u_\epsilon'\to g$ in $L^2(V^*)$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

Choose any sequence $\epsilon_n\downarrow0$ small enough that each convolution is defined on a neighborhood of $[0,T]$, and set $u_n=u_{\epsilon_n}$. Step 5.1 gives both asserted convergences, and step 4.1 gives $u_n'=\eta_{\epsilon_n}*g$. The uniqueness in step 1.1 identifies $g=u'$.

Let $V$ and $H$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective,
continuous linear map with dense range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real linear
dual of $V$. Identify $H$ with its Hilbert dual by its inner product and embed
$H$ into $V^*$ by
$$h\longmapsto\bigl(v\longmapsto (h,i v)_H\bigr).$$
The resulting dense continuous embeddings are written
$$V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^*\hookrightarrow V^*$$
and $(V,H,V^*)$ is called an **evolution triple**. The pairing between $V^*$
and $V$ is denoted $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$.

For a Hilbert space $X$, $L^2(0,T;X)$ is the space of equivalence classes of
strongly measurable $X$-valued functions $w$ with
$$\int_0^T\|w(t)\|_X^2\,dt<\infty.$$
Strong measurability means being an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of
measurable simple functions. For $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$,
say that $g$ is the **weak time derivative** of $u$ when
$$\int_0^T (i u(t),i v)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. The derivative is
unique up to equality almost everywhere. The **parabolic energy space** is
$$W(0,T;V):=\{u\in L^2(0,T;V):u'\in L^2(0,T;V^*)\},$$
with norm
$$\|u\|_{W(0,T;V)}:=\bigl(\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2+ \|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$
No endpoint values are part of this definition; they are assigned only after
a continuous $H$ trace representative has been proved. Separability is an
additional hypothesis when it is needed by a later result.

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $V=\{0\}$, all spaces and maps in the claim are zero and the result holds. Otherwise choose countable dense sets in $V$ and $V^*$, the latter available by [F3]. For fixed $v\in V$, the functional $A(t)v$ has norm at most $M\|v\|_V$. On a countable dense subset $(w_j)$ of the unit sphere, $\|A(t)v-r\|_{V^*}=\sup_j|a(t;v,w_j)-\langle r,w_j\rangle|$ for each fixed $r\in V^*$. Hence these norm distances are measurable. Approximating $A(t)v$ by the first point of a countable dense subset of $V^*$ within $1/n$ gives a measurable countably-valued approximation.

For a.e. fixed $t$ outside the common null set, apply [F4] to $a(t)$ and to its transpose $a(t;w,v)$. Both forms have the same bounds and coercivity because their diagonal values agree. This gives the unique pointwise $x(t)$ and $x^*(t)$ solving the two equations.

Choose a countable linearly independent sequence $(e_j)$ whose linear span is dense in $V$; if $V$ is finite-dimensional, use a finite basis and set $V_n=V$ once it is exhausted. Let $V_n=\operatorname{span}(e_1,\dots,e_n)$. The Galerkin systems for $x_n(t),x_n^*(t)\in V_n$ have measurable matrix entries and measurable right-hand sides. Their matrices are invertible: testing a homogeneous system by its trial vector and using coercivity forces that vector to be zero. Matrix inversion therefore makes the coefficient vectors, and hence $x_n,x_n^*$, strongly measurable.

Truncate the $n$th countably-valued approximation after its first $N_n$ values, replacing the tail by zero. By [F5], choose $N_n$ so the tail set has measure at most $2^{-n}$. These truncations are finite-valued measurable functions; [F6] shows that outside a null set only finitely many tails occur, so they converge pointwise to $A(t)v$. Thus $A(t)v$ is strongly measurable. Applying the same argument to the transposed form proves that $A^*(t)v$ is strongly measurable for each fixed $v$.

For any $z_n\in V_n$, Galerkin orthogonality and coercivity give $$\alpha\|x(t)-x_n(t)\|_V^2\le a(t;x-x_n,x-x_n) =a(t;x-x_n,x-z_n)\le M\|x-x_n\|_V\|x-z_n\|_V.$$ Thus $\|x-x_n\|_V\le(M/\alpha)\inf_{z_n\in V_n}\|x-z_n\|_V$; the identical argument for the transposed form gives the same estimate for $x^*$. Density of $\bigcup_n V_n$ makes both Galerkin sequences converge pointwise to their unique solutions. Their limits are strongly measurable.

Approximate any strongly measurable $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ pointwise a.e. by finite-valued simple functions $u_n$. For each $n$, $A(t)u_n(t)$ and $A^*(t)u_n(t)$ are strongly measurable by step 2.1. The uniform operator bounds give pointwise convergence to $A(t)u(t)$ and $A^*(t)u(t)$ off the common null set, and $\|A(t)u(t)\|_{V^*},\|A^*(t)u(t)\|_{V^*}\le M\|u(t)\|_V$. This proves strong measurability and square integrability of both actions.

Testing each pointwise variational equation by its solution gives $\alpha\|x(t)\|_V^2\le\|q(t)\|_{V^*}\|x(t)\|_V$ and the same inequality for $x^*(t)$. If a solution is zero the claimed bound is immediate; otherwise division by its norm yields the two pointwise estimates. Squaring and integrating proves $x,x^*\in L^2(0,T;V)$ with the asserted bounds.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

$$q_\epsilon(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}\eta_\epsilon(t-s)q(s)\,ds.$$
Then each $q_\epsilon$ is smooth with values in $X$ and
$$\|q_\epsilon-q\|_{L^2(\mathbb R;X)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(\epsilon\downarrow0).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be

derivations.claim: Let $g_1,g_2\in L^2(0,T;X)$ both satisfy the distributional derivative identity for $u$. Put $h=g_1-g_2$ and extend it by zero to $\mathbb R$. For every fixed $x^*\in X^*$ and every interior $t$ farther than $\epsilon$ from the endpoints, the scalar pairing of $\eta_\epsilon*h(t)$ with $x^*$ is zero: it is the zero distribution paired with $s\mapsto\eta_\epsilon(t-s)$. Since continuous linear functionals separate points, $\eta_\epsilon*h(t)=0$. By [F3] these convolutions converge to $h$ in $L^2$ on compact subintervals; exhausting $(0,T)$ proves $h=0$ a.e., so the weak derivative is unique.

The Bochner integral $G(t)=\int_0^t u'(s)ds$ exists by [F2] and [F5]. For each $x^*\in X^*$, scalar Fubini [F4] and integration by parts show that $G$ has weak derivative $u'$. Hence $w=u-G$ has zero distribution derivative. If $\psi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$ has integral zero, its primitive is compactly supported, so $\int w\psi=0$ in $X$. Choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$ with integral one and put $c=\int w\eta$. Subtracting $(\int\psi)\eta$ shows that $w-c$ has zero distribution. As in step 1.1 its interior convolutions vanish, and [F3] makes them converge to $w-c$ locally in $L^2$. Thus $w=c$ a.e. and $u(t)=c+G(t)$ is a continuous representative. Any two continuous representatives equal a.e. agree everywhere, because their continuous difference vanishes on the dense set where they agree; hence this representative is unique.

For fixed $P$, test the weak derivative identity for $u$ against $y^*\circ P\in X^*$ for arbitrary $y^*\in Y^*$. Boundedness of $P$ gives $\int_0^T y^*(Pu(t))\phi'(t)dt =-\int_0^T y^*(Pu'(t))\phi(t)dt.$ The right side is represented by the $L^2(Y)$ function $Pu'$, and uniqueness from step 1.1 gives $(Pu)'=Pu'$.

For the operator-norm $C^1$ family, fix $y^*\in Y^*$ and put $\ell(t)=y^*\circ P(t)\in X^*$, so $\ell'(t)=y^*\circ P'(t)$. Use the representative $u(t)=c+\int_0^t u'(s)ds$ from step 2.1. For $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$, scalar Fubini and integration by parts give $$\int_0^T \ell(t)u(t)\phi'(t)dt=-\int_0^T\bigl(\ell'(t)u(t)+\ell(t)u'(t)\bigr)\phi(t)dt.$$ Indeed, substitute $c+\int_0^t u'(s)ds$ on the left, interchange the integrals over $0\le s\le t\le T$, and use $\int_s^T\ell(t)\phi'(t)dt=-\ell(s)\phi(s)-\int_s^T\ell'(t)\phi(t)dt$; a second Fubini interchange combines the $\ell'$ terms into $\ell'(t)u(t)$. Absolute integrability follows from boundedness of $\ell,\ell',\phi,\phi'$ and [F5]. Since this identity holds for all $y^*$ and $P'u,Pu'\in L^2(0,T;Y)$, the vector-valued weak derivative is $P'u+Pu'$.
The displayed derivative belongs to $L^2(0,T;Y)$ because $P$ and $P'$ are bounded on $[0,T]$ and $u,u'\in L^2(0,T;X)$. Hence $P(t)u(t)\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ with the asserted formula.

Its image is closed: if $J(u_n)\to(u,g_1,\ldots,g_d)$ in $Z$, then for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and every $i$, $$\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi =\lim_n\int_\Omega u_n\,\partial_i\varphi =-\lim_n\int_\Omega D_i u_n\,\varphi =-\int_\Omega g_i\varphi,$$ where each limit follows from Cauchy–Schwarz in $L^2$. Thus $g_i$ is the weak derivative $D_i u$, and the limit lies in the image. A closed subspace of the complete Hilbert space $Z$ is complete in its inherited inner product, so $W^{1,2}(\Omega)$ is Hilbert.

By [F3], $V$ is a closed subspace of $W^{1,2}(\Omega)$, hence Hilbert for the inherited Sobolev inner product. From step 1.1, $$\|
abla v\|_2^2\le\|v\|_{W^{1,2}}^2 =\|v\|_2^2+\|
abla v\|_2^2 \le(1+C_\Omega^2)\|
abla v\|_2^2.$$ Thus the gradient norm is equivalent to the inherited Hilbert norm and is also complete; the norm chosen for $V$ in the Statement is the inherited $W^{1,2}$ norm.

Since $W^{1,2}(\Omega)$ is a subspace of the separable metric space $Z$, it is separable. For any point $x$ in a relatively open set, choose $\epsilon>0$ such that $B(x,\epsilon)\cap W^{1,2}$ lies in that set. Choose a center $z$ from a countable dense subset of $Z$ with $\|x-z\|<\epsilon/4$, then a positive rational $r$ with $\|x-z\|<r<\epsilon-\|x-z\|$. The relative balls $B(z,r)\cap W^{1,2}$ form a countable base. By [A1], choose one point from every nonempty base member; these points are dense. Apply the same argument to the subspace $V$. By [F5], $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is dense in $H$. It is a subset of $V$ by [F3], so $V$ is dense in $H$. measurable load $g\in L^2(0,T;V_h^*)$ and an initial value $U^0\in V_h$. A

$$\tau_j^{-1}(U^j-U^{j-1},v_h)_H+ \bar a_j(U^j,v_h)=\langle\bar g_j,v_h\rangle_{V_h^*,V_h} \qquad(v_h\in V_h).$$

bounded, and coercive as in
[[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]], with constants
$M$ and $\alpha>0$. For $u\in V$, the equation for the unknown $z_h\in V_h$
$$a(z_h,v_h)=a(u,v_h)\qquad\text{for every }v_h\in V_h$$
is the **Ritz equation**; any solution $z_h$ is called a Ritz projection of
$u$. The item [[lem-parabolic-ritz-projection-well-defined]] proves that for
every $u$ there is exactly one solution, denoted $R_hu$, and that these
solutions define a bounded linear map $R_h:V\to V_h$. The form need not be
symmetric.

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

derivations.claim: If $V_h=\{0\}$, define $R_hu=0$; the Ritz equation, uniqueness, and norm bound are immediate. Otherwise fix a finite ordered basis $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ of $V_h$. Form the square matrix $K_{ij}=a(e_j,e_i)$ and vector $b_i=a(u,e_i)$. If $Kc=0$ and $x=\sum_jc_je_j$, then $a(x,e_i)=0$ for each $i$, hence $a(x,x)=\sum_i c_i a(x,e_i)=0$. Coercivity [F2] gives $x=0$, so basis independence gives $c=0$. Thus $K$ has zero kernel and, being square, is invertible. Its unique solution $Kc=b$ defines the unique $R_hu$ satisfying [F1].
Testing [F1] with $v_h=R_hu$ gives $\alpha\|R_hu\|_V^2\le a(R_hu,R_hu)=a(u,R_hu) \le M\|u\|_V\|R_hu\|_V.$ If $R_hu=0$, the bound is immediate; otherwise divide by $\alpha\|R_hu\|_V$.

For $u,w\in V$ and real scalars $c,d$, bilinearity shows that $cR_hu+dR_hw$ satisfies [F1] for $cu+dw$. Uniqueness from step 1.1 gives $R_h(cu+dw)=cR_hu+dR_hw$. The norm bound from step 2.1 proves boundedness, so $R_h$ is the required linear map.

Let $V$ and $H$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective,
continuous linear map with dense range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real linear
dual of $V$. Identify $H$ with its Hilbert dual by its inner product and embed
$H$ into $V^*$ by
$$h\longmapsto\bigl(v\longmapsto (h,i v)_H\bigr).$$
The resulting dense continuous embeddings are written
$$V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^*\hookrightarrow V^*$$
and $(V,H,V^*)$ is called an **evolution triple**. The pairing between $V^*$
and $V$ is denoted $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$.

For a Hilbert space $X$, $L^2(0,T;X)$ is the space of equivalence classes of
strongly measurable $X$-valued functions $w$ with
$$\int_0^T\|w(t)\|_X^2\,dt<\infty.$$
Strong measurability means being an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of
measurable simple functions. For $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$,
say that $g$ is the **weak time derivative** of $u$ when
$$\int_0^T (i u(t),i v)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. The derivative is
unique up to equality almost everywhere. The **parabolic energy space** is
$$W(0,T;V):=\{u\in L^2(0,T;V):u'\in L^2(0,T;V^*)\},$$
with norm
$$\|u\|_{W(0,T;V)}:=\bigl(\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2+ \|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$
No endpoint values are part of this definition; they are assigned only after
a continuous $H$ trace representative has been proved. Separability is an
additional hypothesis when it is needed by a later result.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]], and let
$u,v\in W(0,T;V)$. Each has a unique representative in $C([0,T];H)$, and
for all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr,$$
$$(u(t),v(t))_H-(u(s),v(s))_H =\int_s^t\bigl(\langle u'(r),v(r)\rangle_{V^*,V} +\langle v'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\bigr)\,dr.$$
Writing $c_i=\|i:V\to H\|$, the trace obeys
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_H^2 \le \frac{c_i^2}{T}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2 +2\|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Every bounded sequence in a separable real Hilbert
space $X$ has a weakly convergent subsequence. If $V$ is a separable real
Hilbert space, then $L^2(0,T;V)$ and $L^2(0,T;V^*)$ are separable real Hilbert
spaces, their product is a separable Hilbert space, and the graph of the weak
time-derivative operator is closed there. Consequently $W(0,T;V)$ is a closed
Hilbert subspace of that product and every bounded sequence in $W(0,T;V)$ has
a weakly convergent subsequence.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let $T>0$, and let
$q\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$. Suppose $a(t;\cdot,\cdot)$ is real bilinear and
$t\mapsto a(t;v,w)$ is measurable for each fixed $v,w\in V$. Assume there
is one null set outside which
$$|a(t;v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad a(t;v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$$
for all $v,w\in V$, with $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$. For a.e. $t$ outside
that null set define $A(t)v\in V^*$ and $A^*(t)v\in V^*$ by
$$\langle A(t)v,w\rangle=a(t;v,w),\qquad \langle A^*(t)v,w\rangle=a(t;w,v).$$
Then, for every $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$, both $t\mapsto A(t)u(t)$ and
$t\mapsto A^*(t)u(t)$ are strongly measurable and belong to
$L^2(0,T;V^*)$. For a.e. $t$, the two equations
$$a(t;x(t),v)=\langle q(t),v\rangle,\qquad a(t;v,x^*(t))=\langle q(t),v\rangle\qquad(v\in V)$$
have unique solutions. The solution functions $x,x^*$ are strongly
measurable, belong to $L^2(0,T;V)$, and satisfy
$$\|x(t)\|_V,\ \|x^*(t)\|_V\le\alpha^{-1}\|q(t)\|_{V^*}\quad\text{a.e.}$$
On the exceptional null set set all operator actions and solutions to zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let
$b:X\times Y\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded bilinear form. Suppose there is
$\beta>0$ such that
$$\sup_{\|y\|_Y\le1}|b(x,y)|\ge\beta\|x\|_X\qquad(x\in X),$$
and the only $y\in Y$ satisfying $b(x,y)=0$ for every $x\in X$ is $y=0$.
Then, for every bounded linear functional $F:Y\to\mathbb R$, there is a
unique $x\in X$ such that $b(x,y)=F(y)$ for every $y\in Y$, and
$$\|x\|_X\le\beta^{-1}\|F\|_{Y^*},\qquad \|F\|_{Y^*}:=\sup_{\|y\|_Y\le1}|F(y)|.$$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and let $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]]) satisfy
$$\int_\Omega g\,\varphi\,dx=0\qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$$
([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]). Then $g=0$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$. Moreover, if $g$ is real-valued and $\int_\Omega g\varphi\,dx\ge0$ for every nonnegative $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, then $g\ge0$ almost everywhere.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $V=\{0\}$, density in $H$ forces $H=\{0\}$, and the only data and solution are zero, so the conclusion holds. Assume henceforth $V\ne\{0\}$. By [F1], $W(0,T;V)$ has the stated graph norm. Set $Y=L^2(0,T;V)$ and $X=\{w\in W(0,T;V):w(0)=0\}$, with the inherited $W$ norm. By [F3], $W$ and $Y$ are Hilbert spaces; by the trace bound in [F2], $X$ is a closed Hilbert subspace. Define $$b(w,y)=\int_0^T\bigl(\langle w'(t),y(t)\rangle_{V^*,V} +a(t;w(t),y(t))\bigr)\,dt.$$ The integrand is measurable by [F4], and Cauchy–Schwarz and the form bound give $|b(w,y)|\le(1+M)\|w\|_{W}\|y\|_Y$.

For $w\in X$, let $z_0(t)$ solve $a(t;z_0(t),v)=\langle w'(t),v\rangle$ and set $z=z_0+\mu w$, where $\mu=M^4\alpha^{-4}$. By [F4], $z_0\in Y$ and $\|z_0\|_Y\le\alpha^{-1}\|w'\|_{L^2(V^*)}$, so $\|z\|_Y\le C_z\|w\|_W$ with $C_z=\alpha^{-1}+\mu$. Since $A(t)z_0(t)=w'(t)$, coercivity and the operator bound give $\langle w',z_0\rangle=a(t;z_0,z_0)\ge\alpha M^{-2}\|w'\|_{V^*}^2$. The energy identity [F2] and $w(0)=0$ give $\int_0^T\langle w',w\rangle=\frac12\|w(T)\|_H^2$. The remaining mixed term obeys $|a(t;w,z_0)|\le(M/\alpha)\|w\|_V\|w'\|_{V^*}$, and Young's inequality bounds it by $\frac{\alpha}{2M^2}\|w'\|_{V^*}^2+ \frac{M^4}{2\alpha^3}\|w\|_V^2$. Therefore $$b(w,z)\ge\frac{\alpha}{2M^2}\|w'\|_{L^2(V^*)}^2+ \frac{M^4}{2\alpha^3}\|w\|_{L^2(V)}^2+ \frac{\mu}{2}\|w(T)\|_H^2\ge c_0\|w\|_W^2,$$ where $c_0=\min\{\alpha/(2M^2),M^4/(2\alpha^3)\}>0$. For $w\ne0$, positivity forces $z\ne0$, and $b(w,z)\le\|z\|_Y\sup_{\|y\|_Y\le1}|b(w,y)|$ together with $\|z\|_Y\le C_z\|w\|_W$ gives $\sup_{\|y\|_Y\le1}|b(w,y)|\ge(c_0/C_z)\|w\|_W$; the inequality is trivial for $w=0$.

Suppose $y\in Y$ and $b(w,y)=0$ for every $w\in X$. By [F4], $g(t):=A^*(t)y(t)$ belongs to $L^2(0,T;V^*)$. Taking $w(t)=\phi(t)v$ for $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$ in $b(w,y)=0$ gives $\int\phi'(t)(iv(t),iy(t))_H+\phi(t)a(t;v,y(t))\,dt=0$. By [F1], this means $y'=g$ weakly, so $y\in W(0,T;V)$. Testing the weak derivative identity against $t\phi$ and expanding $(t\phi)'$ shows that $w(t)=t y(t)$ has weak derivative $y+t y'$. Its $H$ trace at zero is zero, so $w\in X$. Substituting this $w$ and using $y'=A^*y$ gives $$0=b(ty,y)=\int_0^T\bigl(\|y(t)\|_H^2+2t\,a(t;y(t),y(t))\bigr)\,dt \ge\int_0^T\|y(t)\|_H^2+2t\alpha\|y(t)\|_V^2\,dt.$$ Hence $y=0$ in $Y$, proving the trivial right-kernel condition.

The preceding steps verify the boundedness, inf-sup and right-kernel hypotheses of [F5]. Consequently, for every $g\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$ the functional $y\mapsto\int_0^T\langle g(t),y(t)\rangle\,dt$ has a unique solution $w\in X$ to $b(w,y)=\int\langle g,y\rangle$ for all $y\in Y$. Its boundedness follows from Cauchy–Schwarz.

By density of $V$ in $H$ and [A1], choose $v_n\in V$ with $\|iv_n-u_0\|_H<1/n$. The measurable-action result [F4] gives $g_n=f-A(t)v_n\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$. Let $w_n\in X$ be the solution from step 3.1 for $g_n$, and let $\ell_n(t)=v_n$ be the constant path. Then $u_n=w_n+\ell_n\in W(0,T;V)$ has $u_n(0)=iv_n$ and $b(u_n,y)=\int_0^T\langle f(t),y(t)\rangle\,dt$ for every $y\in Y$.

For $0\le\tau\le T$, test the equation for $u_n$ with $y=\mathbf1_{(0,\tau)}u_n\in Y$. By [F2], coercivity, and $2ab\le\alpha a^2+\alpha^{-1}b^2$, $$\|u_n(\tau)\|_H^2+\alpha\int_0^\tau\|u_n(t)\|_V^2dt \le\|iv_n\|_H^2+\alpha^{-1}\int_0^\tau\|f(t)\|_{V^*}^2dt.$$ The right side is bounded uniformly in $n$. Also $G_n=u_n'+A(t)u_n-f\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$ by [F4]. Testing with $y=\phi v$ shows $\int\phi\langle G_n,v\rangle=0$ for every fixed $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Choose a countable dense subset of $V$, apply [F6] to its scalar pairings, and take the union of their null sets. Outside that null set continuity of $G_n(t)\in V^*$ gives $G_n(t)=0$. Thus $u_n'=f-A(t)u_n$ a.e. and $\|u_n'\|_{L^2(V^*)}\le\|f\|_{L^2(V^*)}+M\|u_n\|_{L^2(V)}$. Together these estimates bound $(u_n)$ in $W(0,T;V)$.

By [F3], a subsequence converges weakly in $W(0,T;V)$ to some $u$. The trace map $w\mapsto w(0)$ is bounded linear by [F2], so weak trace convergence and $iv_n\to u_0$ in $H$ imply $u(0)=u_0$. For every $y\in Y$, $b(u_n,y)=\int\langle f,y\rangle$ and boundedness of $b$ from step 1.1 let us pass to the weak limit, giving $b(u,y)=\int\langle f,y\rangle$. With $G=u'+A(t)u-f\in L^2(V^*)$, testing by $\phi v$ and applying [F6] on a countable dense subset of $V$ as in step 5.1, with [F7] to unite the null sets, proves the pointwise variational equation for a.e. $t$ and every $v\in V$. Testing the limiting identity with $\mathbf1_{(0,\tau)}u$ and using [F2] gives the stated energy estimate for every $\tau\in[0,T]$.

If $u_1,u_2$ are two solutions with the same data, $z=u_1-u_2$ lies in $X$ and satisfies $b(z,y)=0$ for every $y\in Y$. The uniqueness in [F5] applied to the zero functional gives $z=0$. This proves uniqueness.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a matching affine simplicial mesh of $\Omega$ as defined
in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Fix $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and an integer $q\ge1$. On each
cell let $\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q)$ denote the
restrictions to $K$ of $\mathbb K^q$-valued polynomials of total degree at
most $k$. The **broken polynomial space** is the finite product
$$V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:=\prod_{K\in\mathcal T}\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q),$$
viewed as functions defined almost everywhere cell by cell. For an interior
facet $F=K\cap K'$, the **jump** is the difference of the two polynomial
traces, with either fixed ordering of $K,K'$; its vanishing is independent of
that ordering. The **conforming polynomial space** is
$$V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}:=\{v\in V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:v|_{F,K}=v|_{F,K'}\text{ on every interior facet }F\}.$$
The **zero-boundary subspace** consists of those $v\in V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}$
whose polynomial trace is zero on every boundary facet. These are algebraic
definitions. The Sobolev inclusions and the zero-boundary closure conclusion
are proved separately in the corresponding local theorems on matching
piecewise polynomials and zero-boundary values. If $\mathcal T=\varnothing$,
then $\Omega=\varnothing$ by the mesh definition; the empty product is the
zero vector space consisting of the unique empty function, and the trace
conditions are vacuous.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded polyhedral open set with a finite matching
affine simplicial mesh, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $v$ be a real-valued
conforming piecewise polynomial whose polynomial trace vanishes on every boundary
facet. Then
$$v\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega),\qquad \|v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}.$$
Here $W^{1,p}_0$ is the norm closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$; no C1
trace characterization is used.

Let $V_h$ be a finite-dimensional real subspace of an evolution space $V$,
continuously included in $H$. Let $a(t;\cdot,\cdot)$ be real bilinear,
measurable in $t$, uniformly bounded by $M$ and coercive by $\alpha>0$ on
$V_h$. If $f\in L^2(0,T;V_h^*)$ and $u_h^0\in V_h$, then there is a unique
$u_h\in H^1(0,T;V_h)$ with $u_h(0)=u_h^0$ and
$$((u_h)'(t),v_h)_H+a(t;u_h(t),v_h)=\langle f(t),v_h\rangle$$
for every $v_h\in V_h$ and almost every $t$. It satisfies
$$\|u_h(t)\|_H^2+\alpha\int_0^t\|u_h(s)\|_V^2\,ds \le \|u_h^0\|_H^2+\alpha^{-1}\int_0^t\|f(s)\|_{V_h^*}^2\,ds.$$
Here $H^1(0,T;V_h)$ means absolutely continuous $V_h$-valued coefficient
functions whose value and derivative are square-integrable.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded
polyhedral open set with $d\ge1$. Put
$$H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad V=W^{1,2}_0(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad \|v\|_V=\|v\|_{W^{1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
Then $V$ is a separable real Hilbert space, and the inclusion
$V\hookrightarrow H$ is continuous, injective and dense. Consequently
$(V,H,V^*)$ is a real evolution triple in the sense of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]. The gradient norm
$\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ is equivalent to this norm on $V$ by Poincare's
inequality.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Apply [F3] to this $V_h$ and the restricted form/load. It gives a unique $u_h$ satisfying the stated semidiscrete equation and energy estimate.

space, and let $(V,H,V^*)$ be its real evolution triple. Suppose
$a(t;\cdot,\cdot):V\times V\to\mathbb R$ is bilinear and scalar measurable
for each fixed pair $v,w\in V$, and there is one null set outside which
$$|a(t;v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad a(t;v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$$
for all $v,w\in V$, with constants $M>0$ and $\alpha>0$. Let
$f\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$ and $u_0\in H$. Then there is a unique
$u\in W(0,T;V)$ with $u(0)=u_0$ and, for almost every $t$,
$$\langle u'(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}+a(t;u(t),v) =\langle f(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\qquad(v\in V).$$
For every $t\in[0,T]$ it satisfies
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2+\alpha\int_0^t\|u(s)\|_V^2\,ds \le\|u_0\|_H^2+\alpha^{-1}\int_0^t\|f(s)\|_{V^*}^2\,ds.$$
The proof applies BNB to the space-time form. Scalar measurability suffices
because $V$ is separable and the measurable inverse action is proved locally.

Let $V$ and $H$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective,
continuous linear map with dense range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real linear
dual of $V$. Identify $H$ with its Hilbert dual by its inner product and embed
$H$ into $V^*$ by
$$h\longmapsto\bigl(v\longmapsto (h,i v)_H\bigr).$$
The resulting dense continuous embeddings are written
$$V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^*\hookrightarrow V^*$$
and $(V,H,V^*)$ is called an **evolution triple**. The pairing between $V^*$
and $V$ is denoted $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$.

For a Hilbert space $X$, $L^2(0,T;X)$ is the space of equivalence classes of
strongly measurable $X$-valued functions $w$ with
$$\int_0^T\|w(t)\|_X^2\,dt<\infty.$$
Strong measurability means being an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of
measurable simple functions. For $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$,
say that $g$ is the **weak time derivative** of $u$ when
$$\int_0^T (i u(t),i v)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. The derivative is
unique up to equality almost everywhere. The **parabolic energy space** is
$$W(0,T;V):=\{u\in L^2(0,T;V):u'\in L^2(0,T;V^*)\},$$
with norm
$$\|u\|_{W(0,T;V)}:=\bigl(\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2+ \|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$
No endpoint values are part of this definition; they are assigned only after
a continuous $H$ trace representative has been proved. Separability is an
additional hypothesis when it is needed by a later result.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded
polyhedral open set, let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite matching affine
simplicial mesh of $\Omega$, and choose $k\in\mathbb N_0$. Let
$V=W^{1,2}_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with its $W^{1,2}$ norm,
$H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and let $V^*$ be the continuous dual of $V$;
these spaces form the separable real evolution triple proved in
[[lem-parabolic-zero-boundary-sobolev-space-is-separable]]. Let $V_h$ be the
scalar degree-at-most-$k$ conforming polynomial subspace on $\mathcal T_h$
whose polynomial traces vanish on every boundary facet, as defined by
[[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]]. Suppose the real bilinear
form $a(t;\cdot,\cdot)$ on $V$ is scalar measurable and there is one null
set outside which it is bounded by $M$ and coercive by $\alpha>0$ on $V$.
Let $f\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$ and $u_h^0\in V_h$. Then there is a unique
$u_h\in H^1(0,T;V_h)$ with $u_h(0)=u_h^0$ satisfying
$$((u_h)'(t),v_h)_H+a(t;u_h(t),v_h)=\langle f(t),v_h\rangle_{V^*,V} \qquad(v_h\in V_h)$$
for almost every $t$. For every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|u_h(t)\|_H^2+\alpha\int_0^t\|u_h(s)\|_V^2\,ds \le\|u_h^0\|_H^2+\alpha^{-1}\int_0^t\|f(s)\|_{V^*}^2\,ds.$$

Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be a real evolution triple and let $V_h\subset V$ be a
finite-dimensional conforming subspace. In a mesh instance, the algebraic
piecewise-polynomial conventions are those of
[[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]]; the required inclusion into
$V$ is an explicit hypothesis of this definition. Let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be time-independent,
bounded, and coercive as in
[[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]], with constants
$M$ and $\alpha>0$. For $u\in V$, the equation for the unknown $z_h\in V_h$
$$a(z_h,v_h)=a(u,v_h)\qquad\text{for every }v_h\in V_h$$
is the **Ritz equation**; any solution $z_h$ is called a Ritz projection of
$u$. The item [[lem-parabolic-ritz-projection-well-defined]] proves that for
every $u$ there is exactly one solution, denoted $R_hu$, and that these
solutions define a bounded linear map $R_h:V\to V_h$. The form need not be
symmetric.

Let $V_h\subset V$ be finite-dimensional, and let $a$ be a real bounded
coercive bilinear form with constants $M$ and $\alpha>0$. For every $u\in V$
there is a unique $R_hu\in V_h$ satisfying the defining equation of
[[def-parabolic-ritz-projection]]. The map $R_h:V\to V_h$ is linear and
$$\|R_hu\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\|u\|_V.$$
The argument uses only finite-dimensional linear algebra; it adds no choice
axiom.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a separable real Hilbert space and $Y$ a real Hilbert space, and
let $u\in H^1(0,T;X)$ (meaning
$u,u'\in L^2(0,T;X)$ with distribution derivative). It has a unique
continuous representative on $[0,T]$. Let
$P\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$ be a fixed bounded linear map. Then
$Pu\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ and $(Pu)'=Pu'$.

If instead $P:[0,T]\to\mathcal L(X,Y)$ is continuously differentiable in
operator norm, then $P(t)u(t)\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ and
$$\frac{d}{dt}(P(t)u(t))=P'(t)u(t)+P(t)u'(t)\quad\text{a.e.}$$
In particular, a differentiable time-dependent Ritz comparison contributes
the term $P'(t)u(t)$ to its residual derivative.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]], and let
$u,v\in W(0,T;V)$. Each has a unique representative in $C([0,T];H)$, and
for all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr,$$
$$(u(t),v(t))_H-(u(s),v(s))_H =\int_s^t\bigl(\langle u'(r),v(r)\rangle_{V^*,V} +\langle v'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\bigr)\,dr.$$
Writing $c_i=\|i:V\to H\|$, the trace obeys
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_H^2 \le \frac{c_i^2}{T}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2 +2\|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}.$$

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The fixed-map product rule [F4] gives $(P_hu)'=P_hu'$, so $\rho'=P_hu'-u'\in L^2(0,T;V)$. For a $C^1$ family it gives instead $\rho'=P_h'u+P_hu'-u'$. Also $\theta'=u_h'-(P_hu)'$. The residual is an element of $L^2(0,T;V_h^*)$: for each fixed $v_h$, approximate the strongly measurable $\rho$ by simple $V$-valued functions. Scalar measurability of $a(t;w,v_h)$ for each fixed $w$ makes the corresponding simple-function pairings measurable, and the bound [F6] lets their pointwise limits pass to $a(t;\rho(t),v_h)$. The first term $(\rho',v_h)_H$ is measurable as well. Because $V_h$ is finite-dimensional, measurability on a finite basis gives strong measurability of the $V_h^*$-valued residual. Moreover, $\|\mathcal R_h(t)\|_{V_h^*} \le c_i^2\|\rho'(t)\|_V+M\|\rho(t)\|_V,$ so it is square-integrable.

Subtract [F1] from [F2]. Since $u_h-u=\theta+\rho$ and $u_h'-u'=\theta'+\rho'$, the result for each $v_h$ is $(\theta',v_h)_H+a(t;\theta,v_h) =-(\rho',v_h)_H-a(t;\rho,v_h) =-\mathcal R_h(t)(v_h).$ This uses only the variational equations; no commutation of the full evolution operator with $P_h$ is assumed.

Put $v_h=\theta(t)$ in step 2.1 and use [F5]. Coercivity from [F6] and Cauchy–Schwarz/Young give $\frac12\|\theta(t)\|_H^2- \frac12\|\theta(0)\|_H^2+ \frac\alpha2\int_0^t\|\theta(s)\|_V^2ds \le\frac1{2\alpha}\int_0^t\|\mathcal R_h(s)\|_{V_h^*}^2ds.$ Multiplying by $2$ proves the asserted energy bound.

In the time-independent Ritz case, [F3] gives $a(\rho(t),v_h)=a(R_hu(t)-u(t),v_h)=0$ for every $v_h$. By [F4], $\rho'=R_hu'-u'$, which yields the special residual stated above. In the time-dependent case this cancellation has not been assumed, so step 2.1 retains the complete residual, including $P_h'u$ when the comparison varies.

Assume Countable Choice. Assume the real scalar finite-element setting of
[[cor-shape-regular-affine-fe-primal-energy-approximation]], and set
$V:=H^1_0(\Omega)$ with its usual $H^1$ norm. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be the
stated conforming discrete space, let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be the same
bounded coercive form as in
[[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]], and let
$u\in W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)\cap V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ solve the continuous and
discrete equations for the same bounded linear datum $F:V\to\mathbb R$;
assume also that $V_h$ is finite-dimensional. The natural inclusion
$J:V\to L^2(\Omega)$ obeys $\|Jv\|_{L^2}\le\|v\|_{H^1}$. For
$e:=J(u-u_h)$, let $z_e$ be the adjoint solution from
[[thm-aubin-nitsche-l2-error-estimate-under-adjoint-regularity]]. Suppose
there are $s\in(0,1]$, a normed regularity space $R_s\subseteq V$ for $z_e$,
and constants $C_D,C_R$ independent of $h$ and $e$ such that
$$\|z_e\|_{R_s}\le C_R\|e\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
$$\inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|z_e-w_h\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C_D h^s\|z_e\|_{R_s}.$$
Then
$$\|u-u_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le \frac{M^2}{\alpha}C_{\rm FE}C_DC_R h^{r+s}|u|_{W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
Here $C_{\rm FE}$ is the primal interpolation constant and $M,\alpha$ are
the boundedness and coercivity constants of $a$. In a full-adjoint Poisson
branch, one may take $R_1=H^2(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega)$ with the $H^2$ norm,
provided both displayed dual bounds hold. The $h^{r+1}$ rate is conditional
on those bounds and the primal approximation bound; no full-adjoint
regularity is asserted on an arbitrary Lipschitz domain.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded
polyhedral open set with $d\ge1$. Put
$$H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad V=W^{1,2}_0(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad \|v\|_V=\|v\|_{W^{1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
Then $V$ is a separable real Hilbert space, and the inclusion
$V\hookrightarrow H$ is continuous, injective and dense. Consequently
$(V,H,V^*)$ is a real evolution triple in the sense of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]. The gradient norm
$\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ is equivalent to this norm on $V$ by Poincare's
inequality.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear
in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a
bounded polyhedral open set with a matching shape-regular affine simplicial
mesh family $\{\mathcal T_h\}$, and set $h:=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}h_K\le1$.
Fix an integer $r\ge1$. On the reference simplex let
$(\widehat S_d,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ be an unisolvent real scalar
finite element whose polynomial space contains $\mathbb P_r$. Assume each
degree of freedom has a bounded linear extension to
$W^{r+1,2}(\widehat S_d)$, and let $\widehat I$ be its interpolant. Suppose
there is a global map $I_h$ whose restriction to each cell is the affine
pullback of $\widehat I$, and that $I_hu\in V_h$ for the conforming discrete
space $V_h\subset H^1_0(\Omega)$ whenever
$u\in W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega)$, where $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is the
closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ in $W^{1,2}(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). Then a constant $C$ independent of

$$\|u-I_hu\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C h^r|u|_{W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
The global conformity and zero-boundary mapping property of $I_h$ are explicit
hypotheses; this estimate does not assert them for arbitrary degrees of
freedom.

Assume Countable Choice. Assume the real scalar finite-element setting of
[[cor-shape-regular-affine-fe-primal-energy-approximation]], and set

stated conforming discrete space, let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be the same
bounded coercive form as in
[[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]], and let

Then

Here $C_{\rm FE}$ is the primal interpolation constant and $M,\alpha$ are

regularity is asserted on an arbitrary Lipschitz domain.

finite-dimensional conforming subspace. In a mesh instance, the algebraic
piecewise-polynomial conventions are those of
[[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]]; the required inclusion into
$V$ is an explicit hypothesis of this definition. Let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be time-independent,
bounded, and coercive as in

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a separable real Hilbert space and $Y$ a real Hilbert space, and
let $u\in H^1(0,T;X)$ (meaning
$u,u'\in L^2(0,T;X)$ with distribution derivative). It has a unique
continuous representative on $[0,T]$. Let
$P\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$ be a fixed bounded linear map. Then
$Pu\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ and $(Pu)'=Pu'$.

If instead $P:[0,T]\to\mathcal L(X,Y)$ is continuously differentiable in
operator norm, then $P(t)u(t)\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ and
$$\frac{d}{dt}(P(t)u(t))=P'(t)u(t)+P(t)u'(t)\quad\text{a.e.}$$

Assume Countable Choice and the bounded polyhedral mesh setting, spaces,
form and data of [[thm-parabolic-fem-semidiscrete-existence-energy]]. Let $u$
be the continuous solution supplied by
[[thm-parabolic-variational-wellposedness-and-energy-stability]] on the same
evolution triple and let $u_h$ be the corresponding semidiscrete solution.
For this error identity, assume the additional regularity $u\in H^1(0,T;V)$,
meaning $u,u'\in L^2(0,T;V)$ with the unique continuous representative
supplied by [[lem-parabolic-projection-time-product-rule]]. Let
$P_h:V\to V_h$ be a fixed bounded linear
comparison map, define
$$\rho(t)=P_hu(t)-u(t),\qquad\theta(t)=u_h(t)-P_hu(t),$$
and let $\mathcal R_h(t)\in V_h^*$ be the full residual
$$\mathcal R_h(t)(v_h)=(\rho'(t),v_h)_H+a(t;\rho(t),v_h).$$
Then for almost every $t$ and every $v_h\in V_h$,
$$(\theta'(t),v_h)_H+a(t;\theta(t),v_h)=-\mathcal R_h(t)(v_h),$$
and for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|\theta(t)\|_H^2+\alpha\int_0^t\|\theta(s)\|_V^2ds \le\|\theta(0)\|_H^2+ \alpha^{-1}\int_0^t\|\mathcal R_h(s)\|_{V_h^*}^2ds.$$

time-dependent comparison map $P_h(t):V\to V_h$, with its time derivative

Ritz projection $P_h=R_h$ from
[[def-parabolic-ritz-projection]], Galerkin orthogonality makes
$a(\rho(t),v_h)=0$, so the residual is exactly
$(R_hu'(t)-u'(t),v_h)_H$. If a time-dependent comparison $P_h(t)$ is used,
it must be operator-norm $C^1$; then
$\rho'=P_h'(t)u+P_h(t)u'-u'$, including the projection-derivative term.
For a measurable time-dependent form with a fixed comparison map, no
orthogonality is inferred and the full displayed residual remains.

derivations.claim: For almost every $t$, use the Ritz equation with target $w=u(t)$. It is the conforming Galerkin solution for the bounded functional $F_w(v)=a(w,v)$. By [F1] and [F2], $\|R_hu(t)-u(t)\|_V \le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u(t)-v_h\|_V \le\frac M\alpha C_{\rm FE}h^r |u(t)|_{W^{r+1,2}}.$ Taking the essential supremum proves the first estimate.

The target $w=u(t)$ satisfies the real scalar finite-element hypotheses of [F3]; its Ritz projection is its Galerkin solution for $F_w$. The assumed uniform adjoint constants therefore give $\|\rho(t)\|_H\le C_Ah^{r+s}|u(t)|_{W^{r+1,2}}$. Apply the same argument to $w=u'(t)$ for almost every $t$.

Since $R_h$ is fixed, [F4] gives $\rho'=R_hu'-u'$. The $w=u'$ estimate in step 1.2 bounds $\|\rho'\|_{L^2(H)}$. The canonical embedding $H\to V_h^*$ has norm at most $c_i$, hence $\|\rho'\|_{L^2(V_h^*)}\le c_iC_Ah^{r+s} \|u'\|_{L^2(W^{r+1,2})}$.

For the error splitting $\theta$, the fixed Ritz orthogonality removes $a(t;\rho,v_h)$ from the residual in [F5]. Its initial value is zero because $u_h(0)=R_hu(0)$. inherited $H$ inner product and $V$ norm; a finite-element use instantiates it

bilinear form $a$ on $V$, a load $f\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$, and $U^0\in V_h$.
Put $\bar f_j=\tau_j^{-1}\int_{t_{j-1}}^{t_j}f(t)\,dt$. For
$j=1,\ldots,N$, solve
$$\tau_j^{-1}(U^j-U^{j-1},v_h)_H+ a\!\left(\frac{U^j+U^{j-1}}2,v_h\right) =\langle\bar f_j,v_h\rangle\qquad(v_h\in V_h).$$

There are no interior time jumps; the initial value is the supplied $U^0$.

point value of an $L^2(V^*)$ equivalence class is used. Invalid inputs return

has a unique solution under the stated hypotheses.

When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be a real evolution triple and let $V_h\subset V$ be a
finite-dimensional conforming subspace. In a mesh instance, the algebraic
piecewise-polynomial conventions are those of
[[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]]; the required inclusion into
$V$ is an explicit hypothesis of this definition. Let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be time-independent,
bounded, and coercive as in
[[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]], with constants
$M$ and $\alpha>0$. For $u\in V$, the equation for the unknown $z_h\in V_h$
$$a(z_h,v_h)=a(u,v_h)\qquad\text{for every }v_h\in V_h$$

$u$. The item [[lem-parabolic-ritz-projection-well-defined]] proves that for
every $u$ there is exactly one solution, denoted $R_hu$, and that these
solutions define a bounded linear map $R_h:V\to V_h$. The form need not be
symmetric.

Let $V_h\subset V$ be finite-dimensional, and let $a$ be a real bounded
coercive bilinear form with constants $M$ and $\alpha>0$. For every $u\in V$
there is a unique $R_hu\in V_h$ satisfying the defining equation of
[[def-parabolic-ritz-projection]]. The map $R_h:V\to V_h$ is linear and
$$\|R_hu\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\|u\|_V.$$

axiom.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The four triangles each have area $1/4$, have disjoint interiors, and meet in whole edges or vertices; their union is the closed unit square. The piecewise barycentric coordinate $\phi$ is zero on the boundary and agrees on shared edges. An affine polynomial on each triangle is determined by its three vertex values; matching traces make shared vertex values agree. Thus a global continuous P1 function is determined by the five mesh vertex values. The four boundary values vanish, leaving only the center value, so $V_h=\operatorname{span}\{\phi\}$. By [F3], $\phi\in H^1_0(\Omega)$; $u_0=\phi^2$ is also a continuous zero-boundary piecewise polynomial and lies in $H^1_0(\Omega)$. The norm and form hypotheses follow from [F4].

On a triangle $K$ of area $A=1/4$, the affine map from the reference triangle has determinant magnitude $2A$. If $\lambda$ is the barycentric coordinate of the center vertex, direct integration gives $\int_K\lambda^m dx=2A\int_0^1\int_0^{1-x}(1-x-y)^m dy\,dx =2A/((m+1)(m+2))$ for $m=1,2,3$. Summing over the four triangles yields $\int_\Omega\phi=1/3$, $\int_\Omega\phi^2=1/6$, and $\int_\Omega\phi^3=1/10$. The altitude from the center to each opposite boundary edge is $1/2$, so the barycentric coordinate has gradient magnitude $2$ and $|\nabla\phi|^2=4$ on each triangle. Hence $a(\phi,\phi)=4$ and $a(\phi^2,\phi)=2\int_\Omega\phi|\nabla\phi|^2=8/3$.

Write the orthogonal projection as $P_hu_0=p\phi$. Its defining equation $(u_0-p\phi,\phi)_{L^2}=0$ gives $p=(1/10)/(1/6)=3/5$. By [F5], the Ritz projection is $R_hu_0=r\phi$ with $a(u_0-r\phi,\phi)=0$, hence $r=(8/3)/4=2/3$.
Therefore $P_hu_0-R_hu_0=(3/5-2/3)\phi=-\phi/15\ne0$, since $\phi(c)=1$. If $u_h(0)=P_hu_0$, the error-splitting variable $\theta(0)=u_h(0)-R_hu_0$ is exactly this nonzero function.
